entries.title: Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a tale of literary obsession, with cameos from real-life authors
entries.summary: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and BlissThe protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their e
entries.content:
The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.

No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.

Sophie lurks in the wings of her own life, too. She likes her job but she has much to be sad about. Not long ago, her husband brought their relationship to an end with oafish callousness (she was in the shower; he didn’t bother to take his earbuds out while he delivered the news), and with it her hope of becoming a mother. Now her beloved books are in storage in the garage of her old house and she’s living alone in a dingy rental flat owned by her husband: “The water in Sophie’s glass tasted like pipes. She felt very tired … The coffee table was actually a cable spool with ‘12 AWG’ spray-painted on the drum.”

Mason’s prose is wan and witty, handling the admixture of pathos and bathos well; and her sinuous sentences capture the wavering movements of thought with less fuss and more laughs than, say, Virginia Woolf. As a bookish person, and one inhabiting a lightly metafictional narrative, Sophie is glumly aware of her literary analogues. There’s “a lot of sad girl fiction” on her Kindle. “Eleanor Oliphant,” she reflects. “That was the worst. Even though it was extremely well written and Sophie had recommended it to about 10 people when it first came out, in this moment, she wished she’d never heard of it and couldn’t recall the cheese scones and those cappuccinos Eleanor always ordered, the saddest of all the coffees.”

Mason is brilliant, too, at describing the small but intense joys of everyday life – getting your scalp massaged at the hairdresser, for instance, or owning one really nicely designed pair of trousers. She’s likewise good at life’s routine humiliations and inanities, such as bumping into your ex with a leaky bottle of coconut water in your handbag, or asking a favour from someone whose text messages you have been ignoring, or realising how much it’s going to cost to take an Uber back from Ikea.

The engine of the plot is a parasocial relationship but an old-fashioned one: Sophie becomes obsessed with a famous writer. (The writer is just “the author” for the first part of the book but then, perhaps finding the conceit unwieldy, Mason gives her a name, Lilac Dunne.) Sophie rereads her books, talks to an imaginary version of Lilac, and spends hours scrolling images of her and listening to her on podcasts. Then fantasy and reality collide when, to Sophie’s terror, Lilac is booked to appear after Elizabeth Strout drops out of an event.

An infatuation with the idea of Lilac, with her public persona and her authorial voice, is complicated by a first glancing and then apparently deepening encounter with the real thing. Lilac takes Sophie up, a little, and Sophie is flattered and flustered. She thinks of herself as a nobody but Lilac seems not to. And then … well, no spoilers.

If there’s a fault to be identified in this continuously witty and touching narrative, it’s in the person of Lilac. As a writer she appears to be unstuffy, poised, wise and at ease in the world; Sophie isn’t the only one to fall for her. When we encounter Lilac in person, she’s harder and more ruthless than her public persona but no less impenetrable, with none of the psychological complexity or vulnerability displayed elsewhere. She’s more deus ex machina in Sophie’s story than fully realised character.

But perhaps that’s by design. In this Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper, Mason is nothing if not knowing. As she writes in one of the closing chapters, opening a little postmodern mise en abyme: “If someone wrote a novel about Sophie, which they wouldn’t, but if they did, it could end there.” It doesn’t.

entries.title: Children’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novels
entries.summary: Poetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and moreSmall Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders, Phaidon, £7.95Refrigerator is EMPTY. Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.The Flying Machine of Dreams by Kate Wakeling, illustrated b
entries.content:
Small Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders, Phaidon, £7.95

Refrigerator is EMPTY. Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.

The Flying Machine of Dreams by Kate Wakeling, illustrated by Viviane Schwarz, Otter-Barry, £12.99

A delectable picture-book collaboration that perfectly distils the wonder of the everyday, from the textures of a leaf to a squishy-cushioned den. Wakeling’s irresistible poetry is richly heightened by Schwarz’s sweet, strange illustrations.

The Weather Shop by Thomas Lee, translated by Deborah Smith, Do Re Mi, £12.99

Translated from Korean, this intricate, inviting, Scarryesque picture book features a shop full of rain balloons, cloud pillows and snow sprays (and a sunshine scarf to warm everyone after the blizzard).

Bison Rule, OK! by Sarah Ziman, illustrated by Nia Havilliard, Otter-Barry, £8.99

What annoyed Big Sister this week? What’s the cure for everything in the school medical room? And what’s so good about having a bison as your friend? Witty, satisfying, resonant and fun, this enticing poetry collection will tempt a range of 6+ readers.

African Queens by Onyinye Iwu, Walker, £12.99

From Hatshepsut, the pharaoh her successors tried to erase, to Amanirenas, the Sudanese queen who fought the Romans and won, these strikingly illustrated stories of bold and fearless African rulers will grip 7+ history buffs.

The Palace of Facts by Kate Olesin, illustrated by Andy Smith, What on Earth Books, £22

This gigantic, spectacularly colourful nonfiction treasury is crammed with 400 facts, displayed in the Hall of Mirrors, the Fossil Hall, the Aquarium, the Maze (“The world’s largest maze, in Yancheng, China, is designed in the shape of an elk”) and many more. A rainy-day delight for trivia mavens of 7 or 8+.

Stableheart: Helping Hero by Nicci Johnson, S&S, £7.99

Sad to leave her foster parents and the pony she loved to ride, Pres isn’t yet ready to trust her Aunty Janelle, or form a new bond with the rescue pony at the city stables. But what if he really needs her? This heartwarming, layered, readable story will please 8+ horse lovers and Jacqueline Wilson fans.

How to Steal the Future by Christopher Edge, Macmillan, £7.99

At the heart of a dangerous, ever-changing maze hides the Avenir, a mystery with the power to unlock the future. Drew is looking for his sister Evie, who disappeared during her own attempt to reach the centre. As the traps and puzzles get deadlier, can Drew find Evie and save his own future before time runs out? A high-concept, brain-twisting 9+ thrill ride from the author of Escape Room.

Wilomina: The Land of Dreams and Nightmares by John Chalmers and Sandra Marrs, Scholastic, £9.99

On her way to visit Mum in hospital, a weird train ride strands Wilomina in a parallel world of dreams, where she befriends a talking cat, seeks out a mysterious library, and begins metamorphosing into a ferocious werepire. Fabulously odd, with a colour scheme of visceral purples and lurid greens, this surreal, gripping graphic novel will appeal to 9+ Ghibli fans.

My Name Is Zayn by Fidan Meikle, Floris, £7.99

After a long, dangerous journey fleeing the Taliban, Zayn is wrenched away from his best friend Samim when their dinghy sinks in the English Channel. Sent to a hotel housing other asylum seekers, Zayn’s attempts to start a new life are disrupted when his roommate disappears … A standalone companion to the award-winning My Name Is Samim, this moving, compelling 10+ story of courage and adaptability shines a searchlight on the asylum system and gangs who prey on vulnerable children.

Traitors’ Nest by Frances Hardinge, Macmillan, £16.99

In the kingdom of Thaletal, castles move as a Great Game is played, disrupting the lives of ordinary people. When teenage Burr’s village is threatened by an ominous new castle, a coup attempt backfires and Burr finds himself spirited away to an unknown corner of Thaletal. Can Burr and his sisters – and the strange heiress Burr has unwillingly kidnapped – learn to beat the players at their own Game? Humane, complex and inimitably inventive, this magnificent 12+ fantasy is yet another barnstormer from the Costa-winning Hardinge.

Cut Him Out in Little Stars by Lucy Strange, Chicken House, £8.99

When her fighter pilot fiance is shot down, heartbroken Juliet is sent to stay by the sea with her sister. But the discovery of a local girl’s body plunges her into mysteries past and present, and meeting handsome, scarred flight lieutenant Bertie Campbell complicates everything even more. Can Juliet overcome trauma and terror to risk falling in love again? This enchanting, atmospheric, poignant second world war romance is the brilliant Strange’s first foray into writing for teenagers.

Encore by Miles Toriko Burks, Farshore, £12.99

Kindergarten besties Clayton Noguchi and Aron Santos fell out in middle school; now they’ve unwillingly reunited in senior theatre class. As they navigate improv, drama games and conversations in and out of school, will they end up as friends – or something more? Based on a popular Webtoon, this funny, touching, addictive queer YA graphic novel should delight Heartstopper fans.

Hell to Pay by Lora Beth Johnson, Hot Key, £8.99

Accomplished thief Elle Fields steals secrets from the Dead, just like her brother used to, until a botched attempt cost him his soul. When charismatic stranger Rook offers her a commission promising a chance at resurrection, she can’t resist assembling her former crew for one last Afterlife heist. But there are things Elle doesn’t know about her brother’s death, or the job she’s accepted … Original and fast-paced, boasting taut characterisation and impressive emotional heft, this supernatural YA thriller will electrify Leigh Bardugo devotees.

entries.title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French family
entries.summary: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie FrançaiseWhen Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis,
entries.content:
When Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis, was there too, in a wheelchair, only half aware of what was going on. This 400-page memoir, translated into English by John Lambert, is a homage to both parents and the unlikely history that brought them together. It’s also an act of reparation towards Hélène, whom Emmanuel worshipped as a child but upset as an adult by publishing a book that she’d forbidden him to write.

Hélène grew up in stateless poverty in Paris, the daughter of Georges Zourabichvili, whose parents had fled Georgia in 1921, and Nathalie von Pelken, who as a child had six governesses, one for each day excluding Sunday. Though “the magical world of the fallen Russian aristocracy” was the backdrop, conditions were tough, not least after Georges disappeared in 1944, murdered by partisans for alleged Nazi collaboration. Hélène was 15 at the time and unsuccessfully tried to hide the truth about George’s death from her younger brother, Nicolas.

She was determined and highly ambitious. What she couldn’t excel at, she didn’t do. For a time she considered an acting career but found her metier as a Russian historian. It helped that she was charming and attractive, so much so that an Afghan pilot, on a flight from Tashkent to Paris via Tehran, first invited her to the cockpit, then landed the plane in Kabul in order to kidnap her. He kept her there for four days before a couple of US aid workers sneaked her away on a private plane.

By then she was married to Louis, who worked for an insurance company and was often away on business trips. At home Hélène ruled the roost and let Emmanuel and his two sisters sleep around her bed, a setup she called “kolkhoz”, the name for collective farms in the USSR. There was no television or radio; the children were made to read. Her son’s reading was strenuous: from Jules Verne and Alexander Dumas, he moved on to Dostoevsky at 13. His mother brought out his softer side – whenever she went away he’d write long letters saying how “horribly” he missed her.

He felt abandoned when she began receiving phone calls from a “Mr N” and had long furtive conversations with him. No less distraught, her husband threatened to kill himself. Hélène ended the affair to spare Louis but he “lost her love for ever” and moved from the marriage bed to a tiny room. Worse, she more or less stopped speaking to him, a habit that lasted to the end. When diagnosed with cancer and admitted to a palliative care home, she merely told him she’d be away at a conference.

The mother-son relationship remained close until Emmanuel published A Russian Novel, which explored the story of her father, Georges, which she had asked him not to tell (“It’s my story, not yours. Leave him where he is”). Publication was “a family cataclysm”; she blamed her brother Nicolas for helping with it. Though she did eventually forgive Emmanuel, her loyalty to Russia divided them. A week before the invasion of Ukraine she described Putin as “a rational man”, committed to good relations with Europe. Dismayed, Emmanuel visited Georgia, where his cousin Salome Zourabichvili had become president. A trip to Ukraine followed. He remains violently opposed to Putin.

What’s attractive about the book is its intimacy. If Hélène is a grand dame, her son enjoys the role of bon vivant, disclosing his drinking bouts, journalistic forays, failed relationships and blissful third marriage as well as his bipolar disorder. He’d like to write with “filial piety” and both his father’s genealogical research and his uncle Nicolas’s memoirs help him fill out the family story. But he also lets us in on his uncertainties as he proceeds: “what I’m hoping for is the unhoped for. We’ll see.”

His mother loved order and completeness. And at her memorial Macron praised her for finishing the latest Académie dictionary – a 40-year task – with the word zygomatique (an anatomical term). In reality, as she frustratedly told her son, they’d only reached zoo, with 62 more words to come, the last of them zz, onomatopoeia for sleep. She wouldn’t have slept well if she’d known this book was coming, but it’s an epic achievement and an honest, heartfelt account.

entries.title: The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisis
entries.summary: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal MassachusettsArtie Dam is a much-loved history teacher from coastal Massachusetts famed for his white socks and old sneakers and who sees a growing hopelessness in his young students. Not only are they dispirited by the state of the world, but they also believe they won’t be able to ac
entries.content:
Artie Dam is a much-loved history teacher from coastal Massachusetts famed for his white socks and old sneakers and who sees a growing hopelessness in his young students. Not only are they dispirited by the state of the world, but they also believe they won’t be able to achieve their professional dreams. Their feelings of dread and ennui are shared by Artie who is aghast at the imminent re-election of a cruel and divisive leader (who remains nameless).

Artie is also lonely in the company of his wife, Evie, a therapist who comes from a wealthy family and is dismissive of her “soft” spouse. Artie realises he doesn’t truly know Evie, and she doesn’t care to know him. He traces their loss of connection to their son Rob’s car accident a decade ago in which Rob survived but his girlfriend Heather was killed. Such is Artie’s desolation that he contemplates suicide, if only he can find a way of doing it discreetly. But something happens while he is sailing in his boat that changes his mind. Later, a revelation from his son further shifts his perspective on his relationships.

The Things We Never Say is the latest book from Elizabeth Strout which has been longlisted for this year’s Booker prize and which subtly binds together political events and private anxiety to portray a decent man in existential crisis. The reader is the actor Robert Petkoff who conveys Artie’s innate kindness and quiet despair. With that despair comes a realisation that “every single person [holds] within themselves a vast, unknowable universe”.

Available via Penguin Audio, 6hr 35min

Further listening

Lady Gregory’s Toothbrush

Colm Tóibín, Picador, 3hr 3min

Derbhle Crotty reads the Brooklyn author’s 2003 essay on Augusta Gregory, the Irish playwright and folk historian who famously observed how ownership of a toothbrush separated the gentry from the peasant classes.

Biological War: A Scenario

Annie Jacobsen, Transworld Digital, 11hr 13min

An explosion in a laboratory in Siberia has terrible consequences as a deadly pathogen is released into the atmosphere. Jacobsen narrates her thriller about a biological event based on real-life interviews with senior figures in the military, the CIA and Nato.

entries.title: Passage by Colin Thubron review – mortality and memory in a gem of a novel
entries.summary: A terminally ill woman makes a final trip to Egypt in an exquisitely wrought portrait of end-of-life reckoningVirginia Woolf said of Middlemarch that it is one of the few English novels written for grown-up people. In the shallow and infantilising age through which we are living, Colin Thubron dares to assume that his readers are adults. Passage is a very beautiful, very moving, authentic work of
entries.content:
Virginia Woolf said of Middlemarch that it is one of the few English novels written for grown-up people. In the shallow and infantilising age through which we are living, Colin Thubron dares to assume that his readers are adults. Passage is a very beautiful, very moving, authentic work of art. Hardly more than a novella, it sits lightly in the hand, but its emotional and aesthetic weight overtips the balance.

Thubron began his career as a travel writer and a large part of the action of Passage is set in a vividly but economically evoked Egypt. This is not the teeming Egypt of Cairo or Alexandria, but of the countryside, the villages, and the great immemorial tombs and ancient monuments. The best travel writers know that “abroad” is most convincingly evoked not by awed exclamations at the world’s wonders, but by an attitude of relaxed familiarity. Thubron is obviously an old Egypt hand, or at least has the skill to convince us that he is.

The story he tells is both simple and subtle. The main character is Kathleen, an Anglicised Australian actor whose father had emigrated from Slovenia. She is in her 40s, beautiful and gravely ill, and the brief first chapter is a toe-curlingly stark description of an operation on her brain to investigate a tumour which, as we will learn, is incurable.

As it happens, Kathleen’s husband, Robert, is himself a brain specialist, and has elected, unwisely, to be present at the operation, “standing as far away as space allows … He finds himself staring speechless into his wife’s brain. It is a turmoil of ink and crimson coils, faintly pulsing under the surgeon’s instrument.” Kathleen is awake, and answering questions that will help the doctor to identify cancerous tissue.

Robert and Kathleen’s marriage has gone stale; also, it has a historical blemish, since it was Robert’s younger brother, Alan, who first met Kathleen and fell in love with her when they were both in their teens. The one who loved the most was Alan; Kathleen, having returned home to Melbourne, wrote to him more and more infrequently, then not at all. “It was not until six years later that she reappeared, on Robert’s arm.”

Kathleen is a wonderful creation: strong-willed, outspoken, and above all clear-eyed, about herself and others. She knows how ill she is, but is determined not to give in to self-pity and to live her life as fully as she can to the end, even if the end should prove bitter. Although the surgeon advises against it, she insists, only weeks after the operation, on setting off, with Robert and Alan – yes, Alan does seem a glutton for heartache – on the Egyptian holiday that had been planned before she became ill.

One of the most admirable aspects of the book is Thubron’s restraint in exploiting the symbolic possibilities that this journey holds out to him. Egypt, after all, or the parts of it that the travellers visit, is itself a kind of afterworld. “The temple city that was gathering around them, with its unreadable carvings and maimed statues, was a ruined monument to death and memory.”

Death and memory: these are the poles between which Kathleen’s dwindling existence is strung. What for the other tourists are more or less interesting sites, and sights, are for her the points of exit that she must soon step through: “When her eyes adjusted to the dark, she saw in front of her a gold-lit corridor that appeared to reach into infinity. In its walls, painted gods marched or floated through an ocean of hieroglyphs. Above her spread a constellation of stars.”

When she encounters a local guide, the soft-spoken and quietly considerate Ashraf, it seems she is being offered another and surely final chance at love. However, she knows it is an impossibility: “She imagined his hands encountering with horror the sutures under her hair.” What she does not know is that Ashraf, a political activist, is already a marked man, as she is a marked woman, in a different way, and for different reasons.

Passage is an exquisitely wrought novel which, for all its understated, filigree texture, reverberates in the mind with poetic force. The record of Kathleen’s passage from life into the not-life is at once tragic and affirmative. “No matter, she was moving through a sacred theatre where gods and humans transformed into each other, as if they shared one essence, the immortal and the transient interfused.”

entries.title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara Cartland

entries.content:
Barbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m.

Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel.

Anyone expecting this biography of Barbara Cartland to be an amusing takedown of a monstre sacré along the lines of Craig Brown’s witty 2017 decimation of Princess Margaret will be disappointed. Rather, Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study. Sweet has had unfettered access to the cornucopia of material that Cartland left behind at Camfield Place, the Hertfordshire manor house where she lived until her death in 2000 at the age of 98. Conducting a fingertip search of her letters, scrapbooks and typescripts, Sweet has crafted a generous but clear-sighted account of a woman who was too often reduced to the status of a lazy joke.

She was born in 1901 into the lower upper class. On her father’s side she was pure trade. James Cartland and Son was a Birmingham metalworkers turning out umbrella stands, crocodile-shaped inkwells, shelf brackets shaped like sea monsters and “pharaonic letterboxes embossed with meaningless hieroglyphs”. Her adored mother Polly, meanwhile, was Gloucestershire gentry and there had been the usual rows about marrying down. Cartland’s paternal grandfather killed himself when the business went bust and her father retreated into alcoholism, leaving Polly to manage the tricky business of getting her daughter launched into a life the family could no longer afford.

Sweet suggests that this constellation of losses and compensations set the emotional template for Cartland’s adult life. Men were necessary but fragile and certainly best not relied upon. Having come out as a deb in 1919 into a world where there were not enough husbands to go round, Barbara set out to become financially self-sufficient by plunging into the only kind of work for which she was qualified. For the next decade she filed gossipy titbits about young London society to the Express, the Mirror and the Daily Mail.

This was the world of the Bright Young Things, so often written up today as a madcap time of pyjama parties and midnight dashes to the continent. In fact, Cartland’s columns reveal a society still in shock from the first world war: fathers are dead (Cartland lost hers in the trenches in 1918), grand family houses have been sold, divorce is everywhere and life seems impossible without alcohol or drugs. The men whom Cartland stepped out with were not the heart-throb dukes and dashing airmen that she would later write about, but broken people without the language to express their desolation. “My contemporaries were ashamed to show emotion,” she observed with characteristic perception in her 1943 memoir The Isthmus Years. “We had all of us a horror of sympathy.”

So instead she simply carried on with a brittle determination to make the best of things. After plenty of dalliances with men called things like Pingo Langrishe and Nigs Ratendone she made a tactical marriage to a dull man called Alexander McCorquodale who was heir to a printing fortune. When he retreated into drink – shades of her father – she effected a neat swap by divorcing, then marrying his paternal cousin. In this way there was no need to change her surname: she had replaced one Mr McCorquodale with another. It rankled that she never achieved a title until she herself was made a Dame in 1991. By contrast, her ambitious daughter, Raine, managed to insert herself into the peerage not once but three times through each of her carefully strategic marriages.

The only man who really mattered to Cartland was her beloved younger brother, Ronald. They went on holiday together and endlessly discussed the cod-eastern philosophies that were all the rage in the 1920s: Ouspensky and Gurdjieff were favourites and Cartland retained a vague mysticism to the end of her life involving ghosts and spiritual healing. She also believed in flying saucers and the power of honey to cure just about anything.

Brother and sister bonded too over politics, specifically a socially engaged, internationalist Toryism. Barbara bossed Ronald into parliament where he became a leading anti-appeaser. She in turn wrote one of the first of the tiny number of 1930s British novels that dealt specifically with the evils of Nazi antisemitism. Dangerous Experiment (1936) involves the improbable story of Lena Carrington who, after a shipwreck and a spell as the slave of a tribe of thunder-worshippers in the Caucasus, ends up in Germany where she is courted by a Nazi lover. In the end she breaks things off when she sees him mistreating a Jewish refugee.

This, of course, is not the Barbara Cartland that most of us remember from the 80s and beyond. In what Sweet calls her “imperial phase” she was writing novels with paper-thin plots that she endlessly recycled. She was also a relentless self-promoter. Bed linen, candles and towels were all enthusiastically marketed under her name, although with remarkable restraint she drew the line at scented toilet paper. She also pulled off a promotion with Dewhurst the butcher, which offered customers one of six previously unpublished Cartland novels for every £12 they spent. The promotion was not a great success because of the sheer weirdness of “being given a copy of Desire in the Desert with a parcel of mince”.

But when, in a stroke of fortune so improbable that even now it hardly seems real, her daughter, Raine, became Diana Spencer’s stepmother, Cartland sensed new opportunities for cross-pollination. She took to announcing “I invented virgins” and managed to imply that the royal wedding of 1981 was somehow her doing, despite being pointedly not invited. Raine, a chip off the old block, made sure that the gift shop at the Spencer family seat, Althorp, stocked a full run of Barbara Cartlands.

It would be easy to dismiss Cartland as a quirk, an aberration the likes of which we will not see again. But the great triumph of this brilliant book is the way that Sweet embeds her firmly in the economic, political, social and artistic transformations of the 20th century while charting the ways in which she also transcended them. Somehow, and this remains the deep mystery of it all, Barbara Cartland emerges as that rather admirable thing: an entirely self-made woman.
